title: Mark-Making in Mud, Sand & Foam
strapline: The first writing is a big, glorious swirl in something squidgy.
intent: Children make marks freely in sensory materials, building the confidence and control that writing later needs.
Children develop the large arm movements and shoulder strength that come before fine pencil control.
Children discover that marks carry meaning — a swirl, a line, a dot can stand for something they choose.
Children strengthen the muscle memory of early letter shapes through big, whole-body movements.
Children mark-make without fear of getting it wrong — mud and foam wipe clean, so every attempt is safe.
implementation: Offer trays of shaving foam, wet sand, mud, or cornflour gloop and let children draw with fingers first.
Add tools of different sizes — sticks, brushes, combs, spoons — so marks vary and grips develop.
Model making marks alongside, without asking children to copy: big circles, zigzags, up-and-down lines.
Talk about the marks children make and take their meaning seriously: 'tell me about your marks'.
Introduce big vertical surfaces too — foam on a fence, chalk on a wall — for the whole-arm sweep.
Weave in early letter shapes playfully: draw the swoop of a snake for 's', the round of an apple for 'o'.
Keep it pressure-free — no 'letters' expected — so the joy of making marks stays intact.
key_questions: Tell me about the marks you're making.
Can you make a big swirly one? A tiny one?
What does your mark say — what is it about?
Which tool makes the most interesting line?
Can you make a mark that goes all the way round?

impact.text: Children make marks freely and with growing confidence.
Children give meaning to the marks they make.
Children use large movements, building shoulder and arm control.
Children explore a range of tools and grips.
Children begin to form recognisable shapes and early letters.
Children stay absorbed, exploring marks over and over.

enhancements: A vertical foam or chalk board for whole-arm mark-making.
Natural tools — feathers, twigs, pine cones — for varied marks.
A 'dough disco' or 'squiggle while you wiggle' movement warm-up first.
Trays of coloured sand or glitter foam for extra sparkle.
Rollers, combs and stampers to add pattern and texture.
Outdoor mud-writing on paving with big brushes and water.

playing_exploring: Children plunge into the sensory materials and make marks for the joy of it.
They try every tool and surface without fear of a wrong result.
active_learning: Children repeat and refine their marks, absorbed for long stretches.
The wipe-clean surface invites them to try again and again.
creating_thinking: Children decide what their marks mean and represent ideas with them.
They choose tools and movements to make the marks they want.
